name: Receipts — proof-of-submission vault for portal work
one_liner: For small medical-billing companies and clinic billing managers, Receipts sits behind every payer-portal submission — human or bot — and files a timestamped evidence record (what values were entered, the confirmation page, the reference number) so a timely-filing or "we never got it" denial can be answered in 30 seconds instead of a week of screenshot archaeology.
problem: Billing staff at clinics, dental/specialty groups and small RCM firms submit claims, corrected claims, prior auths and appeals through dozens of payer web portals that have no API. Today the "proof" that a submission happened is whatever the biller remembered to do: a PNG dropped in a shared Google Drive folder, a reference number pasted into a spreadsheet column, or nothing at all. When a payer later denies for timely filing (CO-29) or claims it never received the request, the team has to reconstruct history by hand, and when they can't, the balance is written off. The problem is getting worse, not better: teams are now pointing browser agents (Skyvern, Pomerado-style minted integrations, in-house Playwright bots) at the same portals, and a bot that reports "success" after clicking Submit proves execution, not that the portal committed the right values. Research confirmed the split: Skyvern and Pomerado Cloud sell adaptation to UI changes; Blue Prism and Automation Anywhere log sessions and admin events; none of them independently verifies that the portal recorded the intended values and hands you a defensible receipt.
target_customer: Buyer: the owner or ops lead of a 10-150 seat medical billing / RCM outsourcing firm, and the billing manager at multi-site dental, ortho, behavioural-health and DME groups. These are the people who already carry a denials number in their monthly report and already pay per-seat for clearinghouse and portal-bot tools. Secondary buyer later: the compliance/audit owner at larger provider groups who needs a retention-grade trail.
why_now: Three things changed in the last year. (1) Portal work is being handed to agents at scale — Pomerado (YC F26) launched this week turning any site workflow into a typed MCP tool with a free tier of 100 calls/day and $50/mo premium, and Skyvern sells the same for $29-149/mo; the volume of unattended portal submissions is rising fast. (2) Those tools explicitly sell "we auto-repair when the site changes," which is an availability guarantee, not a correctness guarantee — so the failure mode moves from "the bot crashed" (visible) to "the bot submitted something subtly wrong" (silent). (3) CMS-0057-F has pushed prior-auth turnaround and electronic trails up the agenda for 2026, making submission evidence a line item rather than a nicety.
comparables: Skyvern (skyvern.com, free/$29/$149/mo + enterprise) — AI browser automation that adapts to layout changes; sells reliability of execution, not transaction-level proof of what was submitted. Pomerado (YC F26, github.com/Pomerado/pomerado, MIT core; cloud free 100 calls/day, $50/mo premium) — mints a site workflow into a typed API/MCP tool and auto-repairs when the site changes; again, availability not correctness, and it is infrastructure sold to developers, not an evidence product sold to a billing manager. Klivira — payer-portal automation that advertises screenshot evidence of prior-auth confirmations, the closest direct overlap, but tied to its own automation and to Medicare/payer flows rather than being vendor-neutral. ASSERTUS Clearinghouse — centralises insurer acknowledgment receipts for EDI claims; strong on 277CA-style structured acknowledgments, nothing for the web-portal half of the work. Steel (llms.steel.dev) — browser infra for healthcare portals with session replay and action traces, but replay retention is limited and it is a developer component. UiPath/Blue Prism/Automation Anywhere — session and audit logs around the robot; documentation shows no automatic capture of the portal's returned receipt correlated to a business item. The gap: nobody sells a vendor-neutral evidence layer that works whether the submission was made by a human in Chrome or by someone else's bot, and that is bought by the billing manager rather than the developer.
market_note: Estimates, clearly labelled. US denial-management software is estimated around $840M in 2026 (Mordor-style vendor research, not audited); US medical-billing outsourcing services are estimated at roughly $6-8B. Receipts is not trying to own either — the wedge is a per-seat or per-submission add-on. Plausible first pricing: $300-900/month per billing firm (estimate) for up to ~5k evidenced submissions, which is comfortably below the cost of one write-off-heavy month. Research found no credible public per-seat benchmark for RCM software, so treat pricing as a hypothesis to test, not a figure. Willingness to pay is suggested by the fact that firms already buy portal bots ($29-149/mo tier pricing is public at Skyvern) and already pay staff to take screenshots manually.
risks: 1. The evidence may not be the binding constraint — if payers reject screenshot evidence and only accept 277CA/clearinghouse acknowledgments, the product solves an internal anxiety rather than a recoverable-dollars problem. 2. Distribution: selling a browser extension into HIPAA-covered workflows means BAAs, security questionnaires and IT approval at exactly the small firms with no IT. 3. An incumbent closes it cheaply — Klivira already advertises screenshot evidence inside its own portal automation, and any portal-bot vendor could ship "evidence pack" as a checkbox feature; Receipts only survives if being vendor-neutral (covering human submissions and other people's bots) is genuinely valued.
riskiest_assumptions: 1. That lost or missing submission proof — not genuinely late filing — causes enough write-off dollars to justify a budget line. Research found the general cost-to-contest-a-denial figure (~$57 per denial, Premier 2023 survey cited in 2026 guides) and a ~4.8% net-revenue denial benchmark, but nothing isolating "denied because we couldn't prove it." If most CO-29s are genuinely late, the product is a nice-to-have. 2. That a browser extension can legally and technically sit on payer portals without violating terms of use or tripping security controls, and that billing firms will install it across staff machines. 3. That billing managers will accept the one extra click of tagging a submission to a claim; if tagging is skipped, the vault is full of orphan evidence and useless. 4. That screenshots plus field captures are actually accepted by payers in appeals — if payers only honour clearinghouse acknowledgments, the evidence is worth less than claimed.
first_customers: Ten specific targets, reachable this week: (1) owners of 10-50 seat US billing companies listed in the AAPC and HBMA member directories — HBMA members are exactly this buyer; (2) billing managers posting in r/MedicalCodingandBilling and r/CodingandBilling about CO-29 timely-filing denials and lost portal confirmations; (3) the "virtual assistant for prior auth" staffing firms (Staffingly and similar) whose whole product is humans in payer portals and who would resell evidence capture; (4) two or three multi-site dental or behavioural-health groups found via state dental association vendor lists, where one office manager owns the whole portal workflow. Open with: "send me your last five timely-filing write-offs and I'll show you what evidence you would have had."
validation_test: This week: post in two billing subreddits and email 25 HBMA-listed billing firm owners with one question — "In the last 90 days, how many claims did you write off because you couldn't produce proof of timely submission, and what did you do to try to find it?" Pass: 8+ substantive replies and at least 3 that name a dollar figure above $2,000 or describe hunting through Drive folders for screenshots. Fail: replies saying "our clearinghouse reports cover it" or "that never happens to us" — which would mean the pain lives only in web-portal-heavy niches (prior auth, appeals, out-of-network) and the wedge must narrow to those.
build_plan: Narrowest first version: one Chrome extension + one dashboard, for human billers only, on three payer portals, for one billing firm. (1) Extension watches the biller on an allow-listed payer domain; on Submit it captures the serialised form values, a full-page screenshot of the confirmation screen, the URL, the timestamp and any reference number it can regex out. (2) It asks one question — "which patient/claim is this?" — autocompleted from a CSV of open claims the firm uploads. (3) Everything is hashed and written to append-only storage with the claim ID, payer, submitter and timestamp. (4) Dashboard: one row per claim, status submitted / acknowledged / unconfirmed, and a one-click "Denial pack" PDF with the screenshot, the entered values and the hash chain. (5) Weekly digest: "11 submissions last week had no confirmation number captured — these are your exposure." Cut for v1: any automation of the submission itself, EDI/277CA ingestion, bot-agent SDK, EHR/PM integrations, HIPAA BAA-grade infra beyond encrypted storage and a signed BAA with the first design partner, and anything outside those three payers.
reasoning:
Why Receipts won the venture track. Three candidates were on the table and all three were researched. The agent-attribution idea (from @sriramk's post about not knowing which of his agents did what in email and calendar) is genuinely felt, but research showed Microsoft Agent 365 + Purview and Google Workspace Studio are already building agent identity and audit into the platforms the data lives in — that is a closing gap against two of the best-funded players, with no obvious buyer-sized hole, and it is also adjacent to Holdroom and Driftwatch already in the library. The Blueberry-inspired "opt-in messaging compliance" idea collapsed on inspection: Meta's Marketing Messages consent rules are the product, and the buyer is a growth marketer who buys revenue, not compliance. Receipts survived because the gap is specific and I could name it: Pomerado (launched this week) and Skyvern both sell *availability* on third-party portals — "we repair the integration when the site changes" — while Blue Prism and Automation Anywhere logs prove the robot ran. Nobody sells *correctness with evidence* to the person who eats the cost when a submission can't be proved. Klivira is the one real overlap and it bundles evidence inside its own Medicare automation; the vendor-neutral position (works for human submissions and for other vendors' bots) is open. It serves a buyer well outside software development, which the brief required. Scored 7s across the board and no higher: I verified the competitive landscape and the timing, but I could not verify the dollar size of the specific pain — the available data gives cost-per-denial (~$57) and overall denial rates (~4.8% of net revenue) but nothing isolating "written off because we couldn't prove submission." That unverified number is why this is 7.0/watch rather than dig_deeper, and the validation test is aimed squarely at it. Pain type is expressed: billing teams already screenshot portals by hand and already argue CO-29 denials.

Why Shelf won the build track, and why it is a different problem for different people. Receipts is paid infrastructure for a medical billing manager; Shelf is a free static site for developers browsing agent skills. Different bookmarks (the Pomerado/portal thread vs. @jakubkrehel's /teardown skill), different audience, different workflow, no overlap. Among build candidates, the teardown-illustration ideas lost on dependency economics and prior art: Nano Banana Pro has no free tier for image generation ($0.134/image at 1K), SeeCode and Fleck already occupy the exploded-diagram and URL-critique spaces, and the library already holds Partsy and Flatpack, which are the same "photo in, labelled diagram out" move. Shelf costs nothing to run, needs no model in the loop, and matches the taste file's "research papers as a shelf of books" entry almost exactly. Scored 6.8/watch: the honest discount is on buildability and usefulness — the skills.sh v1 API looks auth-gated (401 reported without credentials), so the corpus may need assembling from GitHub, and the return-visit reason is thin until a weekly diff exists. It builds on, but differs from, the library's Skillscope: Skillscope vets one skill you are about to install, Shelf presents the whole corpus as a browsable object for discovery, which is a different moment and a different output. could_grow is true — a maintained, trusted corpus view with capability data is the seed of a skills-supply-chain security product, though that is explicitly not tonight's build.

Both tracks cleared 6, so both are filed with full briefs and specs; Receipts takes the top-level fields on score.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Receipts — proof-of-submission evidence vault for payer-portal work (from the Pomerado launch + the browser-agent reliability thread). KEPT: researched competitors (Skyvern $29-149/mo, Pomerado free/$50/mo, Klivira, ASSERTUS, Steel, Blue Prism/AA audit docs) and found all of them sell execution reliability or admin audit, none sells vendor-neutral transaction-level proof to a non-developer buyer. Non-software buyer, as required.
2. Agent attribution & undo for shared mailboxes/calendars (from @sriramk's "need an agent watching over all my personal agents"). DROPPED: Microsoft Agent 365 + Purview and Google Workspace Studio are shipping agent identity and audit natively in 2026, so the gap closes against two incumbents who own the data; also uncomfortably close to Holdroom and Driftwatch already in the library.
3. Consent-and-compliance layer for Meta Marketing Messages blasts (from the Blueberry Social Broadcasts post). DROPPED: research showed opt-in consent is enforced by Meta itself and is the platform's own gate, not a product; the buyer is a growth marketer who buys ROAS, not a compliance tool, so there is no clear budget owner.
4. Portal-change regression monitor sold to RPA teams (variant of #1 aimed at developers). DROPPED as a thin variation — same workflow as Receipts but sold to the vendor whose bot broke, which is the buyer least motivated to pay, and it overlaps Driftwatch in the library.

BUILD
1. Shelf — the whole public agent-skills corpus rendered as a browsable library shelf with install-scaled spines and capability colouring (from @jakubkrehel's /teardown skill shipping via npx skills add). KEPT: corpus is real and large (5,200+ skills reported; 18,189 installs on the top skill), skills.sh documents the data shape, zero inference cost, matches the taste file's shelf-of-papers entry.
2. URL → exploded UI teardown poster (from the same /teardown bookmark + @Mappletons on interface abstraction levels). DROPPED: Fleck, UXLens and urltodesign.md already cover annotated URL critique, and research found no way to get genuinely layered output from an image model — the result would be a raster picture pretending to be a diagram.
3. Photo → annotated exploded parts diagram. DROPPED as a near-repeat of Partsy and Flatpack already in the library, and Nano Banana Pro has no free API tier ($0.134 per 1K image), which breaks the "free to try, no signup" rule the taste file insists on.
4. Agent-skill capability scanner as a one-input web page. DROPPED: that is Skillscope, already in the library, and Harmonic's skill-scan-io plus two open-source auditors already do it free.
5. Live ecosystem leaderboard of skills by installs. DROPPED: skillselion.com, linkly.ai and skills.sh all already publish exactly this as ranked lists — Shelf only survives because it is a different presentation of the corpus, not another leaderboard.
research_notes:
Budget used: 3 reading calls, 12 venture calls, 7 build calls (22 of 22). No images could be seen; every bookmark with video-only media was judged on its text plus a summary call where the text was too thin.

READING (3): Pomerado (YC F26) — confirmed it mints a typed API/MCP integration from a plain-language task by exploring the site with Chromium, MIT core, cloud free tier 100 calls/day and $50/mo premium, and that its differentiator is auto-repair when a site changes. supermemory learner-1 — confirmed it is external memory for agents with published pricing ($0/$19/$100/$399), which killed a candidate about "memory for ops teams" before it cost any venture budget. Blueberry Social Broadcasts — the summary showed Meta Marketing Messages require explicit opt-in and the platform enforces it, which is what sank that venture candidate. (Cursor Agent SDK was also summarised and treated as context on the crowded agent-dev-tools market rather than as a candidate source.)

VENTURE (12): searched for insurance-portal and freight-portal automation startups, for agent attribution/audit products, and for proof-of-submission products in healthcare, permits and claims. The pivotal findings: (a) a direct comparison showing Skyvern ($29/$149/mo) and Pomerado Cloud sell adaptation to UI change, while Blue Prism and Automation Anywhere documentation shows session and admin audit logs but no automatic capture of the portal's returned receipt correlated to a business item — this is what defined the gap and turned a vague "monitor your browser agents" idea into Receipts; (b) Klivira advertises screenshot evidence of prior-auth confirmations and ASSERTUS centralises EDI acknowledgment receipts, which narrowed the wedge to *vendor-neutral* evidence spanning human and bot submissions; (c) timely-filing (CO-29) proof is a documented, named pain with a recognised evidence hierarchy, but no source isolates the dollars lost specifically to missing proof — so market_pull and pain were capped at 7 and the validation test was rewritten to target exactly that number; (d) a market call returned a ~$840M US denial-management software estimate and ~$6-8B billing-outsourcing services, both labelled as estimates in the brief; (e) the attribution candidate was dropped after a summary showed Microsoft Agent 365/Purview and Google Workspace Studio already building agent identity and auditability. A freight/retail-portal search was run as the alternative non-software buyer and returned no defensible benchmarks, which is why healthcare won the slot.

BUILD (7): confirmed the skills corpus is real and large (5,200+ community skills reported April 2026; security-review at 18,189 installs on skills.sh as of 2026-10-15) and mapped the data access precisely — skills.sh documents /api/v1/skills (leaderboard with install counts), /api/v1/skills/{source}/{skill} (returns files including full SKILL.md) and an audit endpoint, but v1 appears to require authentication with 401s reported for anonymous calls, so the build plan was changed to a committed static snapshot with a GitHub-API fallback and buildability was scored 7 rather than 8. Checked competing directories (skillselion, linkly.ai, agenticskills.io, skillsdirectory.com) and found all present ranked card lists and none shows the corpus as one object or ecosystem-wide capability distribution — that confirmed the presentation gap. Separately checked the teardown-illustration ideas: Nano Banana Pro has no free API tier for image generation (~$0.134 per 1K image, $0.24 at 4K) and cannot emit layered/semantic SVG, and SeeCode, Fleck, UXLens and ScreenDesc already cover the adjacent ground — which is why those candidates were dropped rather than reshaped, and why the capability analysis in Shelf is regex-based with no model in the loop.
prototype_summary: An interactive before/after prototype of "Receipts", contrasting a 20-minute shared-drive hunt that ends in a $1,840 write-off against a sealed submission vault that answers an Aetna timely-filing denial in 28 seconds and catches a bot's silent field mismatch.
